new_statements.quote: Stress falls on the first syllable of a word. Pronounce it a bit louder, longer or higher-pitched. For example, the word toki is pronounced 'TO-kee' and not 'to-KEE'. [...] [Lesson 9, on tokiponized proper names such as ma tomo Isanpu 'Istanbul':] Stress still falls on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Lang, Sonja. 2014. Toki Pona: The Language of Good. Tawhid. Kindle edition ISBN 978-0-9782923-4-8 (print ISBN 978-0978292300). Part 1, Lesson 1 'Letters and Sounds'; also Lesson 9 'Proper Names'.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (146 pp., Internet Archive PDF converter, no printed page numbers). extracted text of PDF p. 12 ("Lesson 1: Letters and Sounds") gives verbatim: "Stress falls on the first syllable of a word. Pronounce it a bit louder, longer or higher-pitched. For example, the word toki is pronounced 'TO-kee' and not 'to-KEE'." PDF p. 32 ("Lesson 9: Proper Names"), after the rule that foreign names are tokiponized and "ma tomo Isanpu is Istanbul": "Stress still falls on the first syllable." Both quotes match the report exactly (only curly vs straight quote marks differ). Front matter confirms the book: "Toki Pona: The Language of Good, Sonja Lang", "Copyright 2014 Sonja Lang (jan Sonja)", "ISBN: 978…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word, including adapted foreign proper names; realized by greater loudness, length and/or higher pitch. Corroborated independently by Blahuš 2011: 52, 'Der Akzent liegt immer auf der ersten Silbe' (the accent always falls on the first syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None; Lesson 9 explicitly extends the rule to proper names ('Stress still falls on the first syllable'). Blahuš adds 'immer' (always).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical words incl. proper names); most words are disyllabic (Blahuš 2011: 52). Nothing on phrase-level prominence. Prescriptive statement by the language's creator; Blahuš 2011 is a descriptive sketch by an interlinguist. The scan's Wikipedia quote traces to Blahuš 2011, not directly to Lang.
new_statements.identity_note: Toki Pona is a constructed language (creator Sonja Lang, 2001); Glottolog files it under 'Artificial Language', macroarea North America, country CA. There are no dialects; the statement is the creator's canonical rule in the 2014 official book ('pu'), the reference standard the ISO 639-3 request (2021-043) names as the foundation of the language. Glottolog lists zero descriptive references (only the three ISO change requests).

new_statements.quote: Toki Pona's syllables all follow a pattern: consonant + vowel + optional n. If a syllable is at the beginning of a word, the consonant is optional. (For example, ali and unpa don't begin with consonants.) The optional n is forbidden if the next syllable begins with m or n. Four combinations are forbidden due to difficulty hearing and/or saying them; these are: ji, ti, wo, and wu. Accent is always on the first syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (stress) always falls on the first syllable of the word; no conditions, no exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe standard Toki Pona as defined by Sonja Lang (Kisa); jan Pije's lessons are the widely used community tutorial and follow Lang's 120-word standard. No dialectal variety is at issue.
